senses.definition: (dated outside UK and Australia) A man, a fellow.

quotes.text: “Now when I was a little chap I had a passion for maps.”

quotes.text: A chap named Eleazir Kendrick and I had chummed in together the summer afore and built a fish-weir and shanty at Setuckit Point, down Orham way. For a spell we done pretty well.

quotes.text: ‘No. I only opened the door a foot and put my head in. The street lamps shine into that room. I could see him. He was all right. Sleeping like a great grampus. Poor, poor chap.’

quotes.text: If you have Blacks of any kind, brought in of late; Mantoes--Velvet Scarfs--Petticoats--Let it be what it will--I am your Chap--for all my Ladies are very fond of Mourning.

senses.definition: (intransitive) Of the skin, to split or flake due to cold weather or dryness.
(transitive) To cause to open in slits or chinks; to split; to cause the skin of to crack or become rough.

quotes.text: Then would unbalanced heat licentious reign, / Crack the dry hill, and chap the russet plain.
quotes.reference: 1712, Richard Blackmore, Creation: A Philosophical Poem:

quotes.text: whose fair face neither the summer's blaze can scorch nor winter's blast chap.
And then it seems that through the open door there came the chapping of a clock.

quotes.text: The door was shut into my class. I had to chap it and then Miss Rankine came and opened it and gived me an angry look […]

senses.definition: A cleft, crack, or chink, as in the surface of the earth, or in the skin.
(obsolete) A division; a breach, as in a party.

quotes.text: Many clefts and chaps in our council board.
